title: UNIT 2: ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Animals are diverse, eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic organisms.

✓ They respond to stimuli, move, respire, excrete, grow, reproduce and maintain internal conditions.

title: 2.1 CHARACTERISTICS OF ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Animals are:
✓ Eukaryotic → cells have nuclei.
✓ Multicellular → made of many cells.
✓ Heterotrophic → obtain food from other organisms.
✓ Sensitive → respond to stimuli.
✓ Motile → generally capable of movement.
✓ Respire → release energy from food.
✓ Excrete → remove metabolic wastes.
✓ Grow and reproduce.
✓ Have different forms of body symmetry.

✓ Animals are broadly classified according to the presence or absence of a backbone.

title: 2.2 INVERTEBRATES & VERTEBRATES
notes:
✓ Animals are divided into two major groups:

✓ Invertebrates → lack a backbone or vertebral column.

✓ Vertebrates → possess a backbone and well-developed internal skeleton.

✓ Vertebrates include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

title: 2.2.1 INVERTEBRATE ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Invertebrates are the most diverse animal group and lack a vertebral column.

✓ Many have soft bodies.
✓ Some have an external skeleton (exoskeleton), commonly made of chitin.

✓ They include earthworms, insects, spiders, snails, sponges, jellyfish, lobsters, crabs, sea stars and squid.

✓ The major groups include Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata.

✓ Arthropods include crustaceans, spiders, insects and many-legged forms.

title: 2.2.2 VERTEBRATE ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Vertebrates have a well-developed internal skeleton containing cartilage and a vertebral column.

✓ Axial skeleton → skull, vertebrae, ribs and sternum.
✓ Appendicular skeleton → girdles and appendages.
✓ Closed circulatory system with a heart.
✓ Respiratory organs include gills or lungs.
✓ Centralized nervous system with brain and sensory organs.
✓ Paired kidneys form the main excretory system.

✓ Poikilothermic → fish, reptiles and amphibians.
✓ Homeothermic → birds and mammals.

title: 2.3 REPRODUCTION IN ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Reproduction ensures continuity of animal species.

✓ Two major types:

✓ Asexual reproduction → one parent; no fusion of gametes.
✓ Sexual reproduction → usually two parents; male and female gametes fuse during fertilization.

✓ Sexual reproduction produces offspring containing genetic material from both parents.

title: 2.3.1 ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Asexual reproduction involves a single individual and does not require gamete fusion. It is more common in invertebrates.

✓ Budding → a new organism develops as an outgrowth of the parent.

✓ Fragmentation → pieces of an organism develop into new individuals.

✓ Parthenogenesis → an unfertilized egg develops into offspring.

✓ Examples occur mainly among aquatic invertebrates and some insects and vertebrates.

title: 2.3.2 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Sexual reproduction involves male and female gametes.

✓ Male → produces sperm (haploid, n).
✓ Female → produces eggs/ova (haploid, n).
✓ Fertilization → fusion of sperm and egg forms a diploid zygote (2n).
✓ Produces genetic variation because offspring receive genetic material from both parents.

✓ Fertilization may be internal or external.

title: 2.3.3 REPRODUCTION IN INSECTS — METAMORPHOSIS
notes:
✓ Insects reproduce sexually and undergo development involving major changes called metamorphosis.

✓ Complete metamorphosis:
✓ Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult
✓ Example: honeybee.

✓ Incomplete metamorphosis:
✓ Egg → Nymph → Adult
✓ Example: grasshopper.

✓ Complete metamorphosis has 4 stages; incomplete metamorphosis has 3 stages.

title: 2.3.4 REPRODUCTION IN FROG
notes:
✓ Frogs reproduce sexually and usually use external fertilization.

✓ Female releases eggs into water.
✓ Male releases sperm over the eggs.
✓ Fertilized eggs develop into tadpoles.
✓ Tadpoles undergo metamorphosis and develop into adult frogs.
✓ Eggs are surrounded by a jelly-like covering that helps protect them from drying.
✓ Large numbers of eggs are usually produced.

✓ Frog → external fertilization + aquatic eggs + tadpole + metamorphosis.

title: 2.3.5 REPRODUCTION IN CROCODILES
notes:
✓ Crocodiles reproduce sexually with internal fertilization.

✓ Mating occurs in water.
✓ Fertilized eggs develop inside the female before being laid.
✓ Eggs are laid in nests made of sand or vegetation.
✓ Usually about 10–100 eggs may be deposited depending on species.
✓ Eggs have hard, leathery coverings that protect the developing young.

✓ Crocodile → internal fertilization + leathery eggs + nesting on land.

title: 2.3.6 REPRODUCTION IN BIRDS
notes:
✓ Birds reproduce sexually through internal fertilization.

✓ Most species are monogamous; some are polygamous.
✓ Female birds usually have one ovary.
✓ The ovum enters the oviduct where fertilization and egg formation occur.
✓ Oviduct sections → infundibulum → magnum → isthmus → uterus → vagina.
✓ Egg white forms mainly in the magnum.
✓ Shell membranes form in the isthmus.
✓ Shell forms in the uterus.
✓ Eggs are laid and incubated until development is complete.
✓ Hatching releases the chick.
✓ Parental care may include nest building, protection and feeding.

title: 2.3.7 REPRODUCTION IN RAT
notes:
✓ Rat reproduction represents mammalian sexual reproduction.

✓ Fertilization → internal.
✓ Embryo → develops inside the female uterus.
✓ Male reproductive organs → testes, scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens and penis.
✓ Female reproductive organs → ovaries, oviducts, uterine horns and vagina.
✓ Zygote develops into a blastocyst and implants in the uterine wall.
✓ Placenta → supplies oxygen/nutrients and removes wastes.
✓ Amniotic sac → protects the developing embryo.

✓ Rat → internal fertilization + pregnancy + live birth.

title: 2.5 ANIMAL BEHAVIOR
notes:
✓ Animal behavior includes how animals move, interact with other organisms, respond to the environment and learn. Behavior supports survival and reproduction.

✓ Two major types:
✓ Innate/inherent behavior.
✓ Learned/acquired behavior.

title: 2.5.1 TYPES OF ANIMAL BEHAVIOR
notes:
✓ Innate/Inherent behavior → inborn, genetically determined and independent of experience.

✓ Types:
✓ Instinctive → complex inborn behavior, e.g. spider web building and bird nest building.
✓ Reflexive → rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus.
✓ Orientative → movement/orientation in response to a stimulus.

✓ Learned/Acquired behavior → developed through experience during an animal's lifetime.

✓ Examples:
✓ Habituation → reduced response to repeated harmless stimulus.
✓ Classical conditioning → association between stimuli.
✓ Operant conditioning → behavior influenced by reward or punishment.
✓ Insight learning → solving problems using previous experience/reasoning.
✓ Sensitization → increased response after repeated stimulation.

title: ORIENTATIVE BEHAVIOR
notes:
✓ Taxis → directed movement toward or away from a stimulus.
✓ Positive taxis → toward stimulus.
✓ Negative taxis → away from stimulus.
✓ Example → cockroaches moving away from light.

✓ Kinesis → undirected movement influenced by stimulus intensity.
✓ Example → woodlice changing movement in response to temperature.

title: 2.5.2 PATTERNS OF BEHAVIOR
notes:
✓ Behavioral cycles → responses to periodic environmental changes.
✓ Circadian rhythm → daily cycle such as sleep/wake.
✓ Seasonal behavior → migration and other seasonal activities.

✓ Reproductive behavior → behaviors associated with finding mates, courtship and reproduction.

✓ Social behavior → interactions among members of a group.

✓ Competition → struggle for limited resources such as food, mates or territory.

✓ Territory → area defended by an animal or group.

✓ Communication → exchange of information using sight, sound, touch or chemical signals such as pheromones.

title: 2.6 HOMEOSTASIS IN ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Homeostasis is the self-regulatory process that maintains stable internal body conditions despite external changes.

✓ Main components:
✓ Stimulus → Receptor → Control center → Effector → Response.

✓ Important homeostatic processes:
✓ Thermoregulation.
✓ Osmoregulation.
✓ Blood sugar regulation.

title: 2.6.1 THERMOREGULATION
notes:
✓ Thermoregulation maintains internal body temperature within an appropriate range.

✓ Poikilothermic/Ectothermic animals → body temperature varies with environmental temperature.
✓ Examples: fish, amphibians and reptiles.

✓ Homeothermic/Endothermic animals → maintain relatively constant body temperature using internally generated heat.
✓ Examples: birds and mammals.

✓ Methods of temperature regulation:

✓ Physiological → vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering.

✓ Behavioral → seeking shade/sun, burrowing, swimming, huddling, nesting.

✓ Morphological → insulation such as fur, fat and feathers.

✓ Smaller animals generally lose heat faster because they have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio.

title: 2.6.2 OSMOREGULATION
notes:
✓ Osmoregulation controls water balance, osmotic pressure and electrolyte concentration.

✓ Osmoconformers → body osmotic pressure closely matches the surroundings; examples include starfish, jellyfish and lobsters.

✓ Osmoregulators → actively control internal osmotic pressure; examples include humans and many vertebrates.

✓ Human kidney → main organ of osmoregulation.

✓ Hypothalamus + ADH → regulate water balance.

✓ High body water → more dilute/hypotonic urine.

✓ Low body water → less concentrated urine volume and more concentrated/hypertonic urine.

title: 2.6.3 BLOOD SUGAR REGULATION
notes:
✓ Blood glucose is regulated mainly by two pancreatic hormones:

✓ Insulin → released when blood glucose is high; promotes conversion of glucose into glycogen for storage in the liver → blood glucose decreases.

✓ Glucagon → released when blood glucose is low; promotes conversion of glycogen into glucose → blood glucose increases.

✓ Insulin ↓ blood glucose | Glucagon ↑ blood glucose.

title: 2.6.4 CONTROL OF HOMEOSTASIS
notes:
✓ Homeostasis is controlled mainly through feedback mechanisms.

✓ Negative feedback → reverses the original change and brings a condition back toward the normal set point.
✓ Example: increased body temperature → vasodilation + sweating → heat loss → temperature decreases.

✓ Positive feedback → strengthens the original change and moves the condition further in the same direction.

✓ Negative feedback maintains stability; positive feedback amplifies change.
